data.title: Airbnb Data Analysis Using SQL: End to End Insights on Pricing, Hosts, Demand, and Trends
data.excerpt: A complete breakdown of my Airbnb Data Analysis project using SQL only. This post covers pricing trends, host behavior, neighborhood demand, time-based patterns, and customer engagement using real SQL queries
data.content:
# Airbnb Data Analysis Using SQL  
## SQL Exploration of Pricing, Hosts, Demand, Trends, and Customer Behavior

This blog covers the SQL component of my Airbnb Data Analysis project.  
The dataset contains thousands of Airbnb listings with attributes like price, host details, location, availability, and review history. SQL was the ideal starting point because it allowed me to explore patterns, validate assumptions, and build a strong analytical foundation before moving into Power BI or Python EDA.

This page documents only the SQL analysis.  
Other parts of the project such as dashboards and Python visualizations are covered separately in my portfolio.

---

# 1. Pricing and Revenue Insights  

### Average price across all listings
```sql
SELECT
    ROUND(AVG(price),2) AS "Average Price"
FROM airbnb_listings;
```

### Average price by neighbourhood group
```sql
SELECT 
neighbourhood_group,
ROUND(AVG(price),2) AS "Average Price"
FROM airbnb_listings
GROUP BY neighbourhood_group
ORDER BY "Average Price" DESC;
```

### Highest priced room type
```sql
SELECT
room_type AS "Room Type",
ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS "Average Price"
FROM airbnb_listings
GROUP BY room_type
ORDER BY "Average Price" DESC LIMIT 1;
```

### Neighbourhood with highest revenue potential
```sql
SELECT
neighbourhood,
ROUND(AVG((price * reviews_per_month)::numeric), 2) AS "Average Revenue"
FROM airbnb_listings
GROUP BY neighbourhood
ORDER BY "Average Revenue" DESC LIMIT 1;
```

---

# 2. Host Analysis  

### Hosts with the most listings
```sql
SELECT 
host_name AS "Host Name",
SUM(calculated_host_listings_count) AS "Total Listings"
FROM airbnb_listings
GROUP BY "Host Name"
ORDER BY "Total Listings" DESC LIMIT 5;
```

### Average price and availability by host type
```sql
SELECT 
host_type AS "Host Type",
ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS "Average Price",
ROUND(AVG(availability_365)) AS "Average Availability"
FROM airbnb_listings
GROUP BY host_type
ORDER BY "Average Price" DESC, "Average Availability" DESC;
```

### Hosts with more than 10 listings
```sql
SELECT
COUNT(host_id) AS "Total Hosts"
FROM airbnb_listings
WHERE calculated_host_listings_count >= 10;
```

### Outlier hosts
```sql
SELECT
a.host_name,
a.neighbourhood,
a.price,
ROUND(b.avg_price,2) AS neighbourhood_avg
FROM airbnb_listings a
JOIN (
    SELECT neighbourhood, AVG(price) AS avg_price
    FROM airbnb_listings
    GROUP BY neighbourhood
) b
ON a.neighbourhood = b.neighbourhood
WHERE a.price > b.avg_price
ORDER BY a.price DESC;
```

---

# 3. Location and Demand Patterns  

### Neighbourhood group with most listings
```sql
SELECT
neighbourhood_group,
COUNT(*) AS total_listings
FROM airbnb_listings
GROUP BY neighbourhood_group
ORDER BY total_listings DESC LIMIT 1;
```

### Top 10 neighborhoods by review count
```sql
SELECT
neighbourhood,
SUM(number_of_reviews) AS review_count
FROM airbnb_listings
GROUP BY neighbourhood
ORDER BY review_count DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

### High-demand neighborhoods
```sql
SELECT
neighbourhood,
ROUND(AVG(availability_365),2) AS availability,
ROUND(AVG(price::numeric),2) AS price
FROM airbnb_listings
GROUP BY neighbourhood
ORDER BY availability ASC, price DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

---

# 4. Time and Trend Analysis  

### Monthly price trend
```sql
SELECT
review_month,
ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS avg_monthly_price
FROM airbnb_listings
GROUP BY review_month
ORDER BY review_month;
```

### Month-to-month availability change
```sql
SELECT
review_month,
ROUND(AVG(availability_365), 2) AS avg_monthly_availability,
ROUND(
    AVG(availability_365) -
    LAG(AVG(availability_365)) OVER (ORDER BY review_month), 
2) AS month_over_month_change
FROM airbnb_listings
GROUP BY review_month
ORDER BY review_month;
```

### Listings by review year
```sql
SELECT
review_year,
COUNT(*) AS total_listings
FROM airbnb_listings
WHERE review_year IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY review_year
ORDER BY review_year;
```

### Year with highest reviews per listing
```sql
SELECT
review_year,
ROUND(1.0 * SUM(number_of_reviews) / COUNT(DISTINCT id), 2) AS avg_reviews_per_listing
FROM airbnb_listings
WHERE review_year IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY review_year
ORDER BY avg_reviews_per_listing DESC LIMIT 1;
```

---

# 5. Customer Behavior Analysis  

### Room types with highest engagement
```sql
SELECT
room_type,
ROUND(AVG(reviews_per_month::numeric), 2) AS avg_reviews_per_month
FROM airbnb_listings
WHERE reviews_per_month IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY room_type
ORDER BY avg_reviews_per_month DESC;
```

### Review frequency by neighborhood group
```sql
SELECT
neighbourhood_group,
ROUND(AVG(reviews_per_month::numeric), 2) AS avg_review_frequency
FROM airbnb_listings
WHERE reviews_per_month IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY neighbourhood_group
ORDER BY avg_review_frequency DESC;
```

### Hidden Gems
```sql
WITH stats AS (
    SELECT 
        AVG(price) AS avg_price,
        AVG(reviews_per_month) AS avg_reviews
    FROM airbnb_listings
    WHERE price IS NOT NULL AND reviews_per_month IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT
    id,
    name,
    neighbourhood_group,
    room_type,
    price,
    reviews_per_month,
    number_of_reviews,
    availability_365
FROM airbnb_listings, stats
WHERE price < stats.avg_price
  AND reviews_per_month >= stats.avg_reviews
ORDER BY reviews_per_month DESC, price ASC
LIMIT 20;
```

---

# Summary  
This blog covers only the SQL analysis portion of my Airbnb project.  
SQL helped me explore pricing patterns, host behaviors, neighborhood demand, seasonal trends, and customer engagement.  
These insights form the foundation for the Power BI dashboard and Python EDA stages of the project.

data.title: Power BI DAX Date and Time Cheatsheet For Reporting
data.excerpt: A simple and practical DAX Date and Time Cheatsheet designed to help Power BI users avoid date errors, speed up reporting, and work confidently with essential time functions
data.content:
# Power BI DAX Date and Time Cheatsheet: A Simple Guide for Faster, Accurate Reporting

Have you ever missed a meeting or shown up late because you mixed up the date? It happens to all of us. In Power BI, those mistakes don’t just cause confusion. They break dashboards, distort KPIs, and slow down decision making.

While working with DAX, I often found that **date and time functions** were the biggest source of errors. That’s what pushed me to create a clean, simple **DAX Date and Time Cheatsheet** that helps you get the right results without searching online for hours.

This cheatsheet is designed to be your quick reference for building reliable time intelligence in Power BI.

---

## What's inside

Below are some of the most useful DAX functions that every analyst should know. Each one in my cheatsheet includes syntax, an example using **21 Oct 2025**, and a practical use case so you can apply it immediately.

### TODAY() and NOW()
Use these to return the current date and current timestamp. Ideal for dynamic dashboards that need live updates.

### YEAR(), MONTH(), DAY()
Extract specific components from any date. Useful for grouping by year, filtering by month, or breaking down trends at the day level.

### EOMONTH()
Instantly get the last day of any month. Perfect for financial reporting and period end calculations.

### DATEDIFF()
Calculate the time difference between two dates in days, months, or years. Critical for age analysis, time-to-resolution metrics, and project tracking.

### WEEKDAY() and WEEKNUM()
Find the day of the week or the week number for scheduling, forecasting, or pattern analysis.

### EDATE()
Move forward or backward by a given number of months. Great for rolling forecasts and time comparisons like “same period last quarter.”

---

## Download the Cheatsheet

Want to download the full DAX Date and Time Cheatsheet?  
You can get it directly from my LinkedIn post:

[Download from here](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/sandesharsud_dax-date-time-cheatsheet-sandesh-arsud-activity-7393487473726648320-g7fO)

---

## Why I Built This Cheatsheet

When I started learning DAX, I spent far too much time googling date formulas, reading scattered forums, and testing everything manually. Over time I realized that having a single, precise reference would save hours of effort and reduce reporting errors.

So I compiled all the essentials into one cheatsheet that helps me stay accurate, consistent, and fast while building dashboards.

It’s simple, practical, and something you can rely on whenever your date logic feels confusing.

---

## Final Tip

Save this guide. You’ll find yourself using it every time you work with date and time in Power BI.

If you found this useful and want more content like this, feel free to follow my work and explore more projects on my portfolio
